entities.summary:
Wine (died 675 CE) was a pivotal figure in the nascent Anglo-Saxon Church, serving as the first Bishop of Winchester and later Bishop of London, thereby playing a crucial role in establishing and organizing episcopal sees in southern England during the 7th century. His career spanned a tumultuous period marked by the ongoing Christianization of the Heptarchy and the consolidation of ecclesiastical structures under the authority of figures like Archbishop Theodore of Tarsus. Wine's significance lies in his direct involvement in creating foundational dioceses that would shape the religious and administrative landscape of Anglo-Saxon England for centuries.

Consecrated around 660 CE, Wine initially established the See of Winchester, serving the Kingdom of Wessex under King Cenwalh. This appointment marked a critical step in bringing an organized episcopal presence to the West Saxons, who had only recently embraced Christianity. His tenure in Winchester, however, was not without political complexities; he was reportedly expelled by King Cenwalh, leading to a period of uncertainty. Subsequently, around 666 CE, Wine became Bishop of London, then the capital of the East Saxons and part of the Kingdom of Mercia, likely through the influence of King Wulfhere of Mercia. This dual appointment underscores the fluid political and ecclesiastical boundaries of the era, where episcopal authority often shifted with royal patronage.
